text: Lillian Marie Disney (née Bounds; February 15, 1899 – December 16, 1997) was an American ink artist at the Walt Disney Animation Studios and the wife of Walt Disney from 1925 until his death in 1966. Born in Spalding, Idaho, she grew up in nearby Lapwai on the Nez Perce Indian Reservation, where her father Willard worked as a blacksmith and federal marshal. She was the youngest of ten children, and the family struggled financially; her father died when she was seventeen. After graduating from Lapwai High School, she and her mother moved to Lewiston, where she attended a year of business college before moving to southern California in 1923 to live with her sister Hazel's family. While working as a secretary at the Disney Studio in "ink and paint," she met Walt Disney. The couple married on July 13, 1925, in Idaho at her brother's home, with the wedding officiated by the rector of Lewiston's Episcopal Church of the Nativity; Walt's parents did not attend, and her uncle, chief of the Lewiston Fire Department, gave her away. She wore a dress she made herself. They had two daughters, Diane Marie Disney (1933–2013) and Sharon Mae Disney (1936–1993), the latter of whom was adopted. Disney had ten grandchildren: seven by Diane and her husband (Ron W. Miller), and three by Sharon and her two husbands, Robert Brown and William Lund. Lillian is credited with naming Walt's most famous character, Mickey Mouse, during a train trip from New York to California in 1928, when Walt showed her a drawing of the cartoon mouse and suggested the name "Mortimer Mouse"; she replied that the name sounded "too depressing" and suggested "Mickey Mouse" instead. At the Carolwood Pacific Railroad, Walt named his 1:8-scale live steam locomotive the "Lilly Belle" in her honor, and the parlor car of the Disneyland Railroad and a locomotive on the Walt Disney World Railroad were also named "Lilly Belle" in her honor. Walt Disney Imagineering created "The Empress Lilly," a paddle steamer replica at Walt Disney World in Disney Springs, which was christened on May 1, 1977. Lillian was inducted into the Disney Legends in 2003. Walt Disney died of lung cancer on December 15, 1966, at the age of 65. Lillian later remarried John L. Truyens in May 1969, until his death on February 24, 1981, at the age of 73. In 1987, she pledged a $50 million gift toward the construction of a new concert hall in Los Angeles; after several delays, the Walt Disney Concert Hall opened in 2003, six years after her death. She also helped fund the founding of The California Institute of the Arts. In 1996, she donated $100,000 to the Nez Perce indigenous people to support the buying back of tribal artifacts. In response to a controversial biography, she made a rare public statement about her marriage with Walt: "We shared a wonderful, exciting life, and we loved every minute of it. He was a wonderful husband to me, and wonderful and joyful father and grandfather." Lillian suffered a stroke on December 15, 1997, exactly 31 years after Walt's death, and died the following morning at her home in West Los Angeles at the age of 98. She was interred at Forest Lawn Memorial Park in Glendale, California, alongside her first husband, Walt Disney.
